name: jsColorEngine
baseline: lcms-wasm 1.0.5 (LittleCMS 2.16 compiled to wasm32 with Emscripten); also native LittleCMS 2.18 built with gcc
workload: ICC colour transforms (RGB to Lab, RGB to CMYK, CMYK to RGB, CMYK to CMYK, soft-proof RGB to RGB) on a 5-photograph corpus of 3,939,000 px, 1 M px per iteration, 8-bit in and out, relative colorimetric, one core against one core.
claimed_speedup: WASM SIMD tier vs lcms-wasm in MPx/s: RGB to Lab 119.6 vs 35.9; RGB to CMYK 121.5 vs 35.0; CMYK to RGB 82.0 vs 25.4; CMYK to CMYK 81.3 vs 22.9; soft-proof RGB to RGB 118.9 vs 33.7 (page states 3.2-3.6x on the LUT workflows, 1.8x on the matrix path). Vs native C LittleCMS: 1.82-2.28x on the five LUT workflows, but 0.72x on RGB to RGB matrix (118.8 vs 164.5 MPx/s). Pure-JS tier alone is 0.78-1.08x of native C.
compiler_and_flags: jsColorEngine 1.5.0 and lcms-wasm on Node v24.16.0 (Windows 10 x64); native lcms 2.18 under WSL2 Ubuntu 20.04 with gcc 9.3.0, -O2 for RGB-source workflows and -O3 for CMYK-source and soft-proof (seven CFLAGS sets swept, best per workflow); lcms-wasm is the published npm build, its Emscripten flags are not stated; timing auto-scaled to ~400 ms per batch, median of 5, one process per cell
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7700X (8C/16T), single core (taskset -c 0 for native); 31 GB RAM
tradeoffs: ICC subset in JavaScript: image-path LUT output is within 1 LSB of LittleCMS on 100% of tested samples but only 96.8-99.2% bit-exact. Fast tier needs WebAssembly SIMD (inline WASM, ~115 KB gzip UMD). Worker pool for multi-core. MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft.
caveats: Self-run harness (bench/mpx_summary.js, samples/bench) dated 2026-08-19 on v1.5.0. Host asymmetry stated by the author: JS and lcms-wasm ran on Node under Windows, native C under WSL2 on the same CPU. lcms-wasm build flags were not controlled. Native C beats jsColorEngine on the fused matrix-shaper RGB to RGB path at the time of the run (a later WASM matrix kernel is described as 331 MPx/s but not re-run in the head-to-head). README says ratios under ~1.1x are ties. I did not verify how the WASM kernels are authored (package.json lists wabt as a devDependency).
found_via: npm registry search (registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/search) for 'wasm simd' / 'webassembly faster than js', README scan for speed claims; baseline is an Emscripten-built C library

name: turbores
baseline: ffmpeg.wasm (FFmpeg compiled with Emscripten) and the native FFmpeg 7.1.1 CLI
workload: Apple ProRes decode in frames per second: ProRes 422 HQ at 4K, ProRes 4444 at 1080p, ProRes 422 HQ at 1080p, ProRes 422 Proxy at 1080p; single-threaded and multithreaded; averaged over 10 runs.
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded FPS, TurboRes vs ffmpeg.wasm vs native FFmpeg: 422 HQ 4K 42 vs 13 vs 15; 4444 1080p 128 vs 50 vs 55; 422 HQ 1080p 158 vs 48 vs 57; 422 Proxy 1080p 450 vs 131 vs 161. Multithreaded: 422 HQ 4K 250 vs 84 (ffmpeg.wasm) vs 107 (native) vs 160 (native hardware-accelerated). README: 'more than twice as fast as native FFmpeg'. Ratios of about 2.6-3.4x vs ffmpeg.wasm (single-threaded) are derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16, ./scripts/build-zig.sh --release (WASM SIMD, shared-memory threads); native FFmpeg 7.1.1; ffmpeg.wasm version and build flags not stated; TurboRes 1.2.0
tradeoffs: ProRes decode only (no encode). Needs WebAssembly SIMD; multithreaded speed needs shared memory (cross-origin isolation in browsers). MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft. Bit-exact output claimed.
caveats: Benchmark scripts are public (benchmark/README.md: benchmark-turbores.html, benchmark-ffmpeg-wasm.html, benchmark-ffmpeg-native.sh, test files hosted on an r2.dev bucket) and the CPU is named, but the ffmpeg.wasm build and flags are not, so this is capped at C although close to A. First-party numbers. Repo history visible from June 2026 only.
found_via: npm registry search for 'zig wasm' with README scan for speed claims; found the Performance table comparing against ffmpeg.wasm

name: md4x
language: Zig and C (md4c), compiled to WebAssembly and a Node N-API addon
baseline: markdown-it (JavaScript); also md4w, the earlier Zig/C WebAssembly markdown renderer
workload: renderToHtml and parseAST of a medium markdown fixture, µs per iteration, mitata-style bench in packages/md4x/bench.
claimed_speedup: renderToHtml: md4x.napi 7.38 µs/iter (9.85x faster than markdown-it per the page), md4x.wasm 15.08 µs, md4w 17.40 µs, markdown-it 72.68 µs, so the WASM build is ~4.8x faster than markdown-it (derived from page data). parseAST (medium): md4x.wasm 28.12 µs vs markdown-it 50.44 µs (~1.8x, derived); md4w 23.07 µs is faster than md4x.wasm there. README headline: '~8x faster than markdown-it'.
compiler_and_flags: zig build wasm (output packages/md4x/build/md4x.wasm); default zig build uses ReleaseFast for the CLI, WASM optimisation flags not stated; run with bun 1.4.2 (x64-linux)
tradeoffs: Ships both a native N-API addon and a ~135 KB gzip WASM binary; output AST is the comark format, not markdown-it tokens. Zig library with SAX-like streaming parser.
caveats: Headline '~8x' and the 9.85x figure are for the native N-API addon, not the WASM build. Author notes the parseAST top entries (ox-content, md4x.napi, md4w) are within run-to-run noise and the parsers return different AST shapes. Benchmark code is in the repo and CPU is named, but WASM compile flags are not, so C not A. Bun runs JavaScriptCore, not V8. The sibling md4w is catalogued separately and was within 15% of md4x.wasm in this run.
found_via: npm registry search 'zig wasm' / 'written in zig webassembly', README Benchmarks section

name: zaw (Zero Allocation WASM)
language: Zig and Rust (wasm32) with a TypeScript host
baseline: pure JavaScript loop over a TypedArray (Node/V8 via vitest bench) and Rust wasm-bindgen
workload: JS-to-WASM call overhead for small kernels: XOR of an Int32Array with a scalar (10 to 100,000 elements), Float64Array transfer in and out, and 4x4 Float32 matrix multiplication in batches of 1 to 1000.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Up to 14x faster than pure JavaScript and 7x faster than wasm-bindgen for XOR Int32Array'. Table (zaw vs js / vs wasm-bindgen): 100 elements 6.0x / 6.2x faster; 1,000 elements 11.4x / 6.9x; 10,000 elements 12.8x / 3.3x; 100,000 elements 13.8x / 4.3x; at 10 elements plain JS is 1.6x faster than zaw.
compiler_and_flags: Zig wasm32-freestanding with simd128 via build.zig (optimize mode taken from standardOptimizeOption, not stated); Rust wasm build flags not checked; vitest bench (npm run bench-ts); Node/V8 and wasm-bindgen versions not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core Processor (printed at the top of docs/benchmarks.md)
tradeoffs: Low-level shared-channel protocol: you design input and output bindings per function on both sides. Wins only when per-call overhead dominates or arrays are large enough; not a general wasm-bindgen replacement.
caveats: The headline numbers pick the best of the Zig and Rust rows (Rust: 935,915 vs js 73,132 ops/s at 10,000 elements). In the committed bench output, wasm-bindgen is the fastest of all for Transfer In Float64Array at 10 to 10,000 elements and js beats zaw at 10 XOR elements. 4x4 matmul batch of 1 is only 1.1-1.2x over js. Numbers are first-party, flags partly unstated. Root package.json says ISC while GitHub and npm show Apache-2.0.
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm' README scan (zaw), crates.io search 'zaw' (Rust crate from the same repo); benchmark text in docs/benchmarks.md

name: BoltFFI
baseline: wasm-bindgen (Rust-to-JavaScript glue); on native targets UniFFI
workload: FFI call cost for passing generated data across the Rust-WASM/JavaScript boundary: 100 to 1k particles, locations and trades structs.
claimed_speedup: vs wasm-bindgen (WASM): 1k particles 29,886 ns vs 13,532,530 ns (453x); 100 particles 3,117 vs 748,287 ns (240x); 1k locations 21,931 vs 4,037,879 ns (184x); 1k trades 42,015 vs 5,781,767 ns (138x); 100 locations 2,199 vs 283,753 ns (129x). README headline: 'Up to 450x faster than wasm-bindgen', 'Up to 1,000x faster than UniFFI'.
compiler_and_flags: benchmarks/harnesses/wasm-bench (output dir benchmarkjs) wrapping the same Rust code via both generators; snapshot of v0.24.0 run on macOS CI; Rust flags, Node version and wasm-bindgen version not stated
hardware: Apple M3 for the Swift and WASM results (per benchmarks/README.md); M4 Max for the JVM results
tradeoffs: Own code generator and annotations (#[data], #[export]); WASM uses a wire buffer format that avoids per-field allocation; also targets Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, Python and C. wasm-bindgen is more general (documented by BoltFFI itself as materialising every struct as a JS object).
caveats: First-party microbenchmarks whose functions are trivial constructors and sums chosen to isolate FFI overhead, so the 100x-450x figures are boundary cost, not application speed. The benchmarks README names only an Apple chip, no OS, RAM, warmup or iteration counts. The results table in the main README is a static snapshot; the dashboard repo is stated as source of truth and was not opened.
found_via: crates.io search 'wasm-bindgen alternative' / 'wasm ffi' README scan; description 'Up to 450x faster than wasm-bindgen'

name: svgo.mbt (@rivus/svgo)
workload: SVG optimisation with svgo preset-default (34 plugins), multipass, same plugin set (svgo run with moveGroupAttrsToElems off), same Node process, ms per call over ten corpus files.
claimed_speedup: '3.6x faster than svgo at the median', range 1.7x to 4.8x per file. Table (svgo.mbt wasm-gc vs svgo-js, ms): sketch-icon.svg 0.095 vs 0.286 (3.0x); inkscape-drawing.svg 0.165 vs 0.637 (3.9x); SVG_logo.svg 0.470 vs 1.695 (3.6x); Tux.svg 5.679 vs 12.833 (2.3x); Ghostscript_Tiger.svg 10.096 vs 41.113 (4.1x); World map 10.605 vs 50.433 (4.8x). Output within 1.3% of svgo size.
compiler_and_flags: MoonBit wasm-gc build (188 KB wasm plus 2 KB loader); harness node packages/compare/collect.mjs on Node 24 with svgo 4.1.0; MoonBit toolchain version and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Needs WebAssembly GC and JS String Builtins (Node 24+, Bun 1.4+, Deno 2, Chrome 130+, Firefox 134+, Safari 18.4+). Only the 34 built-in preset-default plugins run; custom JavaScript plugins cannot run inside the wasm module. A native MoonBit CLI is also provided (about 10 ms cold start vs about 160 ms for the svgo CLI).
caveats: First-party numbers, hardware not stated, svgo configured with one plugin option off to match. Very new repo (history from September 2026), 1 star. Output size is within 1.3% of svgo and render difference reported as 0 px.
found_via: npm registry search 'moonbit' (package @rivus/svgo) with README scan; repo README table

name: VectorJSON
language: Zig (simdjson port compiled to WebAssembly SIMD) with TypeScript
baseline: Stock streaming/partial JSON parsers in the Vercel AI SDK, Anthropic SDK, TanStack AI and OpenClaw (JavaScript, run under Bun); JSON.parse for one-shot parsing
workload: Streaming an LLM tool_use JSON block in ~12-character chunks, materialising a partial object on every chunk, payloads of 1 KB to 100 KB.
claimed_speedup: 1 KB: Vercel AI SDK 3.9 ms vs 283 µs (14x); Anthropic SDK 3.3 ms vs 283 µs (12x). 5 KB: Vercel AI SDK 23.1 ms vs 739 µs (31x); Anthropic SDK 34.7 ms vs 739 µs (47x). 50 KB: Anthropic SDK 3.39 s vs 2.7 ms (1255x). 100 KB: Vercel AI SDK 6.1 s vs 6.6 ms (920x); Anthropic SDK 13.4 s vs 6.6 ms (2028x). One-shot: JSON.parse is faster (1 KB 2.16M ops/s vs 1.37K ops/s).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15+ -> WASM -> wasm-opt -> TypeScript pipeline; commands 'bun --expose-gc bench/ai-parsers/bench.mjs' and 'bun --expose-gc bench/parse-stream.mjs'; Zig optimise mode and Bun version not stated
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu x86_64 runner (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Not a JSON.parse replacement: README says JSON.parse wins on one-shot parses of small payloads and is roughly equal at 500 KB+. Wins come from incremental O(n) streaming with a live object versus re-parsing the whole buffer per chunk. WASM SIMD required.
caveats: The 900x-2000x figures come from the baselines' O(n^2) re-parse per chunk, an algorithmic difference rather than raw parse speed. Runtime is Bun (JavaScriptCore), not V8. First-party CI numbers, CPU not named. Includes a vendored zimdjson dependency.
found_via: npm registry search 'zig wasm' with README scan; benchmark table in README

name: blake3-jit
workload: BLAKE3 hashing of 96 B, 512 B, 1 KB, 32 KB and 1 MB inputs in Node.
claimed_speedup: 96 B: 362 MB/s vs 149 MB/s (2.4x faster); 512 B: 748 vs 521 MB/s (1.4x); 1 KB: 811 vs 701 MB/s (1.2x); 32 KB: 1.36 GB/s vs 1.97 GB/s (native wins); 1 MB: 1.38 vs 2.06 GB/s (native wins). README: 'Pure JS beats native Rust for small inputs due to FFI overhead.'
compiler_and_flags: WASM SIMD module is generated at runtime (JIT) for inputs of 4 KB and up; bench/ and microbench/ directories exist; Node version and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Wins only for small inputs where N-API crossing cost dominates; native Rust is faster for 32 KB and larger. No .wasm file shipped (code-generated at runtime), which needs WebAssembly.compile permissions.
caveats: First-party table with no CPU or Node version. The win is against FFI overhead of the native binding, not against a faster hash implementation. The repo has a bench directory whose contents I did not open.
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm simd' / 'hand-written wasm' with README scan; Benchmarks table

name: rsmod-pathfinder
language: Rust (wasm-pack), with AssemblyScript and TypeScript variants benchmarked
baseline: TypeScript implementation of the same breadth-first pathfinder on Node.js; AssemblyScript WebAssembly variant
workload: 100k pathfinding requests on a reconstruction of the Lumbridge map square (64x64 tiles, full clipping flags), destination 10 tiles north with a single access point.
claimed_speedup: Per call: Rust native about 2.8 µs; Rust WebAssembly about 7.0 µs (100k paths in ~700 ms); AssemblyScript WebAssembly about 15.3 µs; TypeScript about 38.5 µs. So Rust wasm is ~5.5x and AssemblyScript wasm ~2.5x faster than TypeScript (derived from page data). cargo bench find_path: 7.19 µs.
compiler_and_flags: Rust release mode on Windows x64 with NodeJS; wasm-pack build --target nodejs; AssemblyScript flags and Node version not stated
tradeoffs: Single-purpose pathfinder for a RuneScape-style tile map; the README also mentions a 'real world' ~850 ms figure for the wasm build on a TypeScript server.
caveats: Repository is archived (read-only). The main.js and main.rs drivers and the TypeScript and AssemblyScript sources are not visible in the repo listing, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from this repo. Synthetic single-map workload; first-party numbers. The ~850 ms 'real world' figure is unexplained.
found_via: npm registry search 'assemblyscript' (package @2004scape/rsmod-pathfinder) with README scan; also on crates.io as rsmod-pathfinder

name: utf-as
language: AssemblyScript (Wasm SIMD with a SWAR fallback)
baseline: AssemblyScript stdlib String.UTF8.decode / String.UTF8.encode (benchmarks run on V8)
workload: UTF-8 decode and encode of 15 HTML payloads from the simdutf corpus, plus UTF-8 and UTF-16 validation throughput over 18 payloads.
claimed_speedup: 'UTF8.decode: 2.1-6.7x faster than String.UTF8.decode on the HTML payloads'; 'UTF8.encode: 4.3-9.4x faster than String.UTF8.encode'; 'UTF8.validate: up to 55.4 GB/s on ASCII-heavy HTML; 11.9-34.4 GB/s on other HTML payloads'; 'UTF16.validate: up to 87 GB/s on surrogate-free HTML'.
compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript asc with --enable simd (SWAR path without it); npm run bench:vs-stdlib and bench:simdutf; also runnable on WAVM and wazero; asc version not stated
tradeoffs: Ported from simdutf westmere SSE4 kernels to 128-bit Wasm SIMD. Small inputs (under 64 bytes) use a SWAR path; the SIMD path needs --enable simd. AssemblyScript only.
caveats: Baseline is AssemblyScript's own String.UTF8 implementation, not JavaScript TextDecoder or a C++/Emscripten library. README states no CPU model; detailed results are chart images in the repo, only the prose ranges are text. Very new (history June to September 2026, v0.4.0), 1 star.
found_via: npm registry search keywords:assemblyscript, README scan for 'faster than'

name: blazediff WebAssembly build (@blazediff/core-wasm)
language: Rust (wasm32 with simd128) with TypeScript glue
workload: Pixel-by-pixel image diff of RGBA buffers on the repo's fixture set (4k, page, blazediff and pixelmatch image pairs), image decode excluded, 25 iterations with 5 warmup.
claimed_speedup: WebAssembly section: '~50.8% performance improvement on average'. 4k/1: pixelmatch 332.26 ms vs core-wasm 33.18 ms (90.0%, ~10x derived from page data); 4k/2: 333.33 vs 68.37 ms; 4k/3: 423.14 vs 44.65 ms (89.4%); blazediff/1: 1.24 vs 0.24 ms. Identical-image pairs are near ties (4k/2 identical 22.70 vs 22.17 ms). Package README: '~51% faster, up to ~16x on 4K'.
compiler_and_flags: Rust compiled to wasm32 with v128 SIMD (+simd128) through wasm-bindgen; Node.js 22; rustc version and opt flags not stated
hardware: Apple M1 Max (per BENCHMARKS.md hardware section), macOS
tradeoffs: Buffers-only API (caller decodes images); ~32 KB wasm plus ~10 KB glue; diff counts agree with pixelmatch within ~0.05% rather than exactly (different YIQ classification at edge cases).
caveats: First-party suite, CPU and Node version stated but compiler flags not. Average improvement (~50.8%) is far below the best rows (90%); the project also ships a JS build (~62.2% average) and a native binary, so the WASM build is one of three variants. Page says byte-identical pairs used to be slower than pixelmatch until a memcmp fix.
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm simd' README scan (@blazediff/core-wasm); benchmarks/pixel-by-pixel.md WebAssembly section

name: sparkdown
baseline: markdown-it and marked (JavaScript, Node) for the WebAssembly build; pulldown-cmark, comrak, cmark for the native build
workload: Render the ~200 KB CommonMark spec (tests/fixtures/data.md) to HTML in one process.
claimed_speedup: Node, same ~198 KB document: sparkdown wasm 0.90 ms vs markdown-it 4.52 ms (5.0x) and marked 5.20 ms (5.7x). Native: sparkdown 0.59 ms vs pulldown-cmark 0.68 ms (1.16x), comrak 2.00 ms, cmark C ~1.9 ms; sparkdown wasm 0.93 ms in the native table. mdast output: ~0.9 ms vs remark (mdast-util-from-markdown) ~73 ms.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench reproduces the sparkdown vs pulldown-cmark pair; harness/ directory holds the compatibility gates and benchmarks; Node version and Rust flags not stated
hardware: Apple Mac Studio (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: 100% CommonMark 0.31.2 conformance claimed; GFM extensions optional; wasm is base64-inlined with zero dependencies.
caveats: First-party, CPU model and Node version not stated; the README also claims to beat rushdown's native build from inside WebAssembly. Very new repo (June 2026), 3 stars. Mostly a Rust library with a wasm build, so the language-level comparison overlaps the wasm-libraries category.

name: sasso
workload: Compile a 138-stylesheet tree (lila's own flags), best of five, measured against the published npm package.
claimed_speedup: 138 stylesheets: npx sasso native engine 266 ms, wasm engine 610 ms, sasso 0.15.0 binary 137 ms, dart-sass 1.104.1 2268 ms, so the wasm engine is ~3.7x faster than dart-sass (derived from page data). README also claims ~19-30x end-to-end for the native binary; sasso/speed WASM entry is stated as ~2x faster than the default size-optimised module.
compiler_and_flags: Published npm package (wasm engine) and release-page binary; bench via 'cd bench && RUNS=12 WARMUP=3 LOOP_N=200 bash scripts/run_bench.sh'; bench/three_way.md holds the full methodology (not opened)
hardware: 12-core machine, macOS arm64 (2026-09-17 run); Linux x86_64 runs dated 2026-10-02; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Sync APIs need synchronous importers; async APIs use an asyncify module. Drop-in for the sass modern API with 62 open issues; not every dart-sass feature may be covered.
caveats: Most of the headline speedups (19-30x) are for the native binary, not WebAssembly; the wasm figure is 610 ms vs 2268 ms. First-party numbers, bench/three_way.md predates the last allocation-reduction round by the README's own note. Very new repo (October 2026 history visible), 7 stars.
found_via: npm registry search 'zig wasm' / wasm README scan (sasso); crates.io search 'wasm' (sasso)

name: sha2-wasm
baseline: hash-wasm (WebAssembly SHA-2 compiled from heavily optimised C); native C built with gcc -O3 -march=native
workload: SHA-256 and SHA-512 compute over 500 MB in RAM, HMAC, PBKDF2 and small hashes, single thread, median of 5 samples, test/bench.ts.
claimed_speedup: '+5-7%' faster than hash-wasm (SHA-256 1.05x, SHA-512 1.07x); about 68% of native C speed. Throughput: SHA-256 217 MB/s, SHA-512 314 MB/s on 500 MB; small hashes ~2.20M ops/s (SHA-256, 55 B).
compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript compiled to a 13.2 KB WebAssembly binary; run with bun run bench (Bun, JavaScriptCore); asc flags and library versions not stated
tradeoffs: Zero-allocation design with static scratchpad in the data segment; SHA-2 and HMAC/PBKDF2 only; README is in Spanish.
caveats: Claim is a 5-7% margin over hash-wasm, which is small enough to be run-to-run noise; CPU described only as 'a modern x86-64 processor'; Bun not V8; hash-wasm version not stated. Brand-new repo (12 commits, July 2026), 1 star. hash-wasm itself is catalogued separately.
found_via: npm registry search keywords:assemblyscript + 'as-' prefix, README scan for 'ops/s' (@edison-manrique/sha2-wasm)
